traveler: Harry Houdini (Erik Weisz, later Ehrich Weiss)
title: Failure Means a Drowning Death: the Rabbi's Son, the Handcuff King, and the War on the Mediums
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rabbi's Son and the Necktie Shop

stops.name: Erzsebetvaros, Budapest, the birth he will spend forty years denying
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Birth date and city from Hungarian Jewish archival birth-record research; no street or building is named in any reachable source, so the pin sits on the historic Jewish quarter rather than a confirmed address.
stops.campa: In the Jewish quarter of Pest a son is born to Mayer Samuel Weisz, rabbi, and Cecelia Steiner. They name him Erik. The house is not recorded; no street, no number, only the city and the date reach the archive. For forty years of professional life the boy will tell reporters, census takers, and biographers that he was born in Appleton, Wisconsin, on the sixth of April, and he will tell it so steadily that the lie outlives him in reference books. Budapest is the first container he gets out of.
suggested_refs: Hungarian Jewish birth registers for Erzsebetvaros, 1874
The 1878 SS Frisia passenger manifest, which carries the family name as Weisz
sources: Adam Begley, Houdini: The Elusive American (2020)

stops.name: Castle Garden, the Battery: Cecelia comes off the Frisia
stops.date_confidence: Date and ship attested from the family's 1878 passenger manifest as cited in modern biographies. Castle Garden as the specific depot is an inference from the port and the year, not a manifest citation, and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Cecelia Weiss comes down the gangway pregnant, with four children and no English, to join a husband who has gone ahead to Wisconsin where a small Reform congregation has offered a pulpit to a man trained in Hungary. The depot at the Battery processes them among the season's hundreds of thousands. The manifest spells the family Weisz. Within a few years the spelling settles as Weiss, and within twenty the fourth child will be answering to a French name he took off the cover of a book. He is four years old.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden immigration depot records, 1878 season

stops.name: Appleton, Wisconsin: the pulpit, and the birthplace he invents
stops.date_confidence: Settlement in 1878 and the father's dismissal in 1882 are attested (PBS; History Museum at the Castle). Month of arrival inferred to order the segment. The five-cent backyard circus is family tradition, dated 1883 to Appleton by the PBS timeline, which conflicts with the same body of sources placing the family in Milwaukee from 1882; the contradiction is left standing. Coordinates are general downtown Appleton, the congregation building being unconfirmed.
stops.campa: Mayer Weiss takes the pulpit of the Zion Reform congregation, a small German-speaking Jewish community on the Fox River, and holds it four years before the congregation dismisses him for a younger man who can preach in English. Appleton will one day name a downtown plaza for him and keep a museum exhibit for a birth that happened in Budapest. Family tradition sets a five-cent backyard circus here, in the yard behind the house, the boy hanging by his knees from a homemade trapeze and billed as Ehrich, the Prince of the Air.
suggested_refs: Zion Reform Jewish Congregation records, Appleton
Houdini Plaza and the Harry Houdini exhibit, History Museum at the Castle, Appleton
sources: History Museum at the Castle, Appleton

stops.name: Milwaukee, the years the family has nothing
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a period, 1882 to 1887, by the PBS timeline and Silverman. Month and day unknown, defaulted. The father's naturalization on 6 June 1882 in Wisconsin is separately attested.
stops.campa: The pulpit gone, the family drops into the poverty that follows an immigrant clergyman with no trade. They move between rented rooms. The children sell newspapers, shine shoes, run errands; the father, learned in Hebrew and Hungarian and German, cannot earn in English. On the sixth of June 1882, in the middle of it, Mayer Weiss becomes a citizen of the United States, and the family goes on moving between rented rooms. Ehrich is eight years old when the bad years start and thirteen when they end.
suggested_refs: Wisconsin naturalization record for Mayer Weiss, 6 June 1882

stops.name: East Seventy-ninth Street, Manhattan: the necktie shop and the book
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted. The PBS timeline names East Seventy-ninth Street as the boardinghouse location but gives no house number, so the pin marks the corridor generally.
stops.campa: The father takes the boy ahead to New York and they board on East Seventy-ninth Street while the rest of the family follows. Ehrich cuts neckties in a shop, runs with an athletic club, meets a fellow cutter named Jacob Hyman, and gets hold of the memoirs of Jean-Eugene Robert-Houdin, the French clockmaker who made himself the first modern conjurer. He reads them the way a hungry man reads a menu. Twenty-one years later he will publish a book proving that most of what is in them is false.
suggested_refs: Jean-Eugene Robert-Houdin, Memoires (1858), the copy that made a necktie cutter into a magician

stops.name: New York City, Ehrich Weiss becomes Harry Houdini
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Wikipedia and the PBS timeline; month and day unknown, defaulted. No venue is recorded for the act's formation, so the pin reuses the family's attested East Seventy-ninth Street address.
stops.campa: With Jacob Hyman he works up a two-man act for dime museums and beer halls and takes a stage name off the book he loves: Houdin, plus an i, on the understanding that this makes it mean like Houdin in French. It does not, and nobody in the audience is French. Ehrich Weiss becomes Harry Houdini at seventeen and answers to it for the rest of his life. Within a year his brother Theodore, called Dash, replaces Hyman, and the two of them bill the act as the Brothers Houdini.
suggested_refs: Dime museum and beer hall billing for the Brothers Houdini, New York, 1891-1893

stops.name: New York, the death of Mayer Samuel Weisz
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by the PBS timeline. The address of the death is not in the reachable record; the pin reuses the family's attested East Seventy-ninth Street boardinghouse and should not be read as the room he died in.
stops.campa: The rabbi dies in New York on the fifth of October, ten years after Appleton and having never held another pulpit anywhere. His son is eighteen years old and takes on the support of his mother, repeating for the rest of his life a promise made at the bedside; he prints his own account of that promise in 1924. From here on he cables her from every city he plays. He buys her a dress said to have been made for Queen Victoria and has her wear it while he watches.
suggested_refs: Houdini's own account of the deathbed promise, repeated in A Magician Among the Spirits (1924)

stops.name: Jackson Park, Chicago: the Columbian Exposition, from the outside
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Wikipedia and Silverman; month inferred to place the stop inside the fair's run, May to October 1893. The sources are explicit that the Brothers Houdini were not a fair attraction.
stops.campa: The Brothers Houdini work the entertainment trade thrown up around the World's Columbian Exposition, hundreds of acts competing for the same crowds along the Midway and in the halls beyond it. Later publicity will imply a triumph. They are not a fair attraction: two obscure young men in the overflow, doing the trunk trick for whatever a manager will pay, in a city holding more magicians per block that summer than any city on earth. The season pays small money.
suggested_refs: Midway Plaisance and the fringe entertainment district of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition

segments.name: Metamorphosis: Bess, the Dime Museums, and Martin Beck

stops.name: Coney Island, Brooklyn: the wedding after three weeks
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. The ceremony site and officiant are not securely documented and sources differ on whether there were civil, Jewish, and Catholic rites or some subset; the venue is therefore tradition, and the pin marks the Coney Island district where she was performing and her family lived.
stops.campa: Wilhelmina Beatrice Rahner sings with the Floral Sisters on the Coney Island circuit and is courted first by Theodore and then, in about three weeks, by Harry. They marry on the twenty-second of June. She is eighteen and Catholic, he is twenty and the son of a rabbi, and the accounts describe both families getting the rite each required. Bess steps into Theo's place in the act. In Metamorphosis she is locked in the trunk and he stands on the lid; the curtain closes, three claps, and the two have changed places.
suggested_refs: The Metamorphosis substitution trunk, bought from the magician Joseph Hartz's stock and used for thirty years

stops.name: Middleton's Clark Street Dime Museum, Chicago: the handcuffs that beat him
stops.date_confidence: Date and venue attested by Wikipedia, which places the defeat at Middleton's Clark Street Dime Museum. The pin is the Clark Street dime museum district near the Loop; the exact storefront is not established, and no contemporary clipping was read this pass.
stops.campa: Between the wedding and the fame come the dime museums: twenty shows a day, the Welsh Brothers Circus in season, medicine tents, and a spiritualist turn he will later disown as the worst thing he ever did for money. In 1898 he prints a catalogue for Harry Houdini's School of Magic, ready to sell off his secrets and quit. Then on the eleventh of January, on the platform at Middleton's, a pair of handcuffs beats him. He cannot get out. It happens in front of a paying room, and no clipping from that day has been found.
suggested_refs: The 1898 catalogue of Harry Houdini's School of Magic
sources: Milbourne Christopher, Houdini: The Untold Story (1969)

stops.name: A beer hall in St. Paul, Minnesota: Martin Beck brings his own irons
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by PBS, 'Houdini and Martin Beck'; month and day are not recorded and are defaulted, so this stop reads as earlier in the year than the January defeat at Middleton's when in fact it came after it. The order is narrative, not documentary.
stops.campa: Martin Beck, booking agent, watches the act in a St. Paul beer hall with other theater men. He is bored by the card work and interested in the cuffs. He tells Houdini to come back the next day and get out of irons that Beck will bring himself, and Houdini does. The telegram that follows offers dates on the Orpheum circuit with one instruction attached: drop the magic, do the escapes. Houdini is twenty-five, has been working dime museums for five years, and does what the telegram says.
suggested_refs: Martin Beck's Orpheum circuit booking telegram, 1899
sources: PBS American Experience, 'Houdini and Martin Beck'

stops.name: New Scotland Yard, Victoria Embankment: he asks to be locked up
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month inferred to order the London season. New Scotland Yard stood on the Victoria Embankment from 1890, so the building is right; the room of the demonstration is not confirmed.
stops.campa: At the police headquarters on the Embankment, Houdini asks to be locked up, and officers of Superintendent William Melville's world put him in irons around a pillar and leave him. He is out before they reach the corridor. He will run the same transaction on police in Berlin, Moscow, Amsterdam, and Chicago for fifteen years, because it converts the state's own instruments into advertising: if the police cannot hold him, the handbill does not have to argue the case. Scotland Yard gives him a certificate, and it stays on his billing on two continents for the next ten years.
suggested_refs: The Scotland Yard certificate, reproduced on Houdini's British and American billing for a decade
sources: CIA historical review, 'Was Houdini a Spy?'

stops.name: Alhambra Theatre, Leicester Square: the London season makes him
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the PBS timeline; month inferred to follow the Scotland Yard demonstration. The salary figure of roughly $300 a week is as given by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: On the strength of the Scotland Yard business the Alhambra on Leicester Square books him, and the engagement is extended, and extended again, and his name stays on the bill through the summer. His salary climbs toward three hundred dollars a week and then well past it. Eighteen months before this he had been printing a catalogue to sell off his secrets and get out of the business, on an American circuit that had nearly finished him. He will not play America again for five years. He is twenty-six years old.
suggested_refs: Alhambra Theatre programmes, London, summer 1900

stops.name: Appellhofplatz, Cologne: the slander trial
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the PBS timeline, with the appeal later the same year; month inferred. Coordinate flagged: the research pool paired the label Landgericht Koln with a coordinate in the Altstadt by the Dom, and the modern Landgericht building is twentieth-century and the wrong site. The 1902 proceedings were heard in the Appellhofplatz courthouse complex; this pin is that complex, not independently re-verified against a Cologne court record.
stops.campa: A policeman named Werner Graff tells the Rheinische Zeitung that Houdini escapes by bribing officials and carrying duplicate keys, and the paper runs it under the headline The Unmasking of Houdini. In Berlin two years earlier the police had watched him and let him go; here the German state calls him a fraud in print. He sues. He opens locks in the courtroom in front of the judge, wins, and wins again when Graff appeals, with a fine and costs against the policeman. He advertises the verdict for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Rheinische Zeitung, 'Die Entlarvung Houdinis', Cologne, 1902
The Cologne court judgment and appeal record, 1902

stops.name: Moscow, out of the Siberian transport van
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted. Wikipedia says only that in Moscow he escaped from a Siberian prison transport van and does not name Butyrka; the Butyrka attribution is itself a reconstruction, and the pool's own two lenses tagged this event differently. Coordinate corrected to the Butyrka figure of 55.7844, 37.5939. Claims of a private performance for Tsar Nicholas II are weaker still and are not carried.
stops.campa: He is stripped, searched, and locked into the steel carette the Russian police use to move prisoners east, and he is out of it in under half an hour. The copy that follows says the van's only key was held in Siberia, so that a failure would have meant being carried there to be let out. Whether the van stood at Butyrka, whether any of the detail is anything but copy, the reachable record does not settle. What it holds is that he performed in Moscow in 1903 and got out of a prison transport.
suggested_refs: Russian police carette transport vans of the period, Butyrka transit prison, Moscow
sources: Milbourne Christopher, Houdini: The Untold Story (1969)

stops.name: London Hippodrome, the Daily Mirror handcuffs
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Date, venue, the crowd of roughly four thousand, the duration of over an hour, and the coat cut away with a knife held in the teeth are all in Wikipedia and the PBS timeline, drawn from contemporary Daily Mirror coverage and Houdini's own diary.
stops.campa: The Daily Mirror produces a pair of cuffs a Birmingham locksmith named Nathaniel Hart says took him five years to build, and four thousand people fill the Hippodrome to see whether they hold. Houdini works inside a small curtained cabinet for over an hour. He comes out twice. He is refused permission to take his coat off and cuts it from his own body with a penknife held in his teeth. When he finally stands up free he weeps on the stage, and Bess kisses him there in front of the house. He is thirty years old.
suggested_refs: Daily Mirror coverage of the Hippodrome challenge, March 1904
Nathaniel Hart's nested handcuff, Birmingham

segments.name: The Challenge Circuit and the Unmasking

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street, Manhattan: the one fixed address
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left standing: Wikipedia gives 1904 and a price of $25,000, the PBS timeline dates the family's move to the Harlem brownstone to 1905. Month and day unknown, defaulted. Coordinate corrected: the pool's pin sat two blocks north; 278 West 113th lies between Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Blvd and Frederick Douglass Blvd.
stops.campa: He buys a five-story brownstone in Harlem, reportedly for twenty-five thousand dollars, and fills it with his mother, his wife, his brothers, and what becomes the largest private library of magic and psychical research in the world. There is a room for the books, a room for the apparatus, and a bathtub he uses to practice holding his breath. He has been in continuous motion since he was thirteen and this is the only address of his adult life. He will die in a hospital in Detroit.
suggested_refs: The Houdini collection of magic and psychical research, acquired by the Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin, in 1958

stops.name: The United States Jail, Washington: out of Guiteau's cell
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the PBS timeline, which states outright that he escaped from the jail that once held President Garfield's assassin, so the Guiteau detail is carried on the cited source rather than dismissed as legend. Month and day unknown, defaulted. No primary jail record was reached. Coordinate corrected to the old United States Jail at 19th and B Street SE; the pool's pin was about a kilometre northwest.
stops.campa: Stripped, searched, and locked into a cell in the federal jail on the Anacostia side of the city, Houdini is out of it in a couple of minutes. Then he opens the other cells along the block, moves the prisoners into each other's, and lets himself out through the corridor door. He hands the story to the evening papers the same day, as an assessment of what the government's locks are worth. The keepers had put him, deliberately, in the cell that once held Charles Guiteau, who shot President Garfield.
suggested_refs: The old United States Jail, 19th and B Street SE, Washington, demolished in the twentieth century

stops.name: Rochester, New York: the bridge jump goes on film
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the PBS timeline, which specifies that his first filmed manacled bridge jump was captured at Rochester. Month and day unknown, defaulted. The specific bridge is not named by the source; the Genesee crossings are the obvious candidates but the identification is a reconstruction, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: Manacled, he goes off a bridge over the Genesee in front of thousands standing on the banks, and comes up holding the irons. The bridge jump is the cheapest item in the repertoire and the most useful: no theater, no admission, no apparatus, no percentage to a house manager, and a story in the evening paper of whatever town he is playing that week. This time a camera is running, so the crowd that watched it free can be sold the same thirty seconds indoors. Which of the Genesee crossings he jumped from, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Surviving footage of Houdini's manacled bridge jumps, 1907 onward

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street: The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested by the PBS timeline; month and day unknown, defaulted. Conjurers' Monthly Magazine, founded 1906, is attested by Steinmeyer and consistent with the magazine's known 1906 to 1908 run. The book was written and researched from the Harlem house, so the pin is the brownstone; no separate editorial address is recorded.
stops.campa: From the brownstone he runs Conjurers' Monthly Magazine for two years, using it to settle scores and to assert his own priority in the history of the craft. He also researches, in newspapers and playbills and patent records across Europe, the career of the man whose name he took at seventeen, and finds that most of the inventions Robert-Houdin claimed were other men's. Then he prints what he found. He is at pains to say that he did not take it from other writers on magic.
stops.quote: Stripped of his self-woven veil of romance, Robert-Houdin stood forth, in the uncompromising light of cold historical facts, a mere pretender, a man who waxed great on the brainwork of others.
stops.quote_source: Harry Houdini, The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin (New York, 1908)
suggested_refs: Conjurers' Monthly Magazine, New York, 1906-1908
Jean-Eugene Robert-Houdin, Memoires, the book the Unmasking dismantles
sources: Harry Houdini, The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin (1908), Project Gutenberg #42723
Jim Steinmeyer on Conjurers' Monthly Magazine

stops.name: St. Louis, Missouri: Failure Means a Drowning Death
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the Milk Can Escape debut to 25 January 1908 but names no city. St. Louis as the debut city rests on the PBS timeline and Silverman and is carried but not overstated. The theater is not identified in any reachable source, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: An oversized galvanized can is filled with water on the stage, Houdini is handcuffed and lowered into it, the overflow goes across the boards, and the lid is padlocked down. A curtain closes over the whole thing. The poster outside says: Failure Means a Drowning Death. Audiences are invited to hold their breath along with him, and discover at forty seconds what he is supposedly still doing at two minutes. He is out well before the water could kill him. The can is real and so is the water.
suggested_refs: The Milk Can Escape poster, 'Failure Means a Drowning Death', lithographed c. 1908

stops.name: Outside Hamburg: the biplane leaves the ground
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Smithsonian Air and Space, 'The Hunt for Houdini's Airplane', and by contemporary reporting. The parade ground outside Hamburg is not more precisely located in the reachable sources, so the pin is the city.
stops.campa: He buys a French Voisin biplane and hires a mechanic named Antonio Brassac to keep it running. In training on the parade ground outside Hamburg he wrecks it, and the machine goes back for repair before he tries again. On the twenty-sixth of November it leaves the ground with him in it. He is thirty-five years old, has never flown anything before buying this machine, and has been in the aviation business for a matter of weeks. Nothing about it is an escape and nothing about it is a trick.
suggested_refs: Houdini's Voisin biplane, its later fate uncertain
Smithsonian Air and Space, 'The Hunt for Houdini's Airplane'
sources: Smithsonian Air and Space, 'The Hunt for Houdini's Airplane'

stops.name: Diggers Rest, Victoria: three flights over a paddock
stops.date_confidence: Date contradiction left standing: 18 March 1910 is the commonly cited date, the Jewish Virtual Library gives 16 March. Priority contradiction also left standing: Colin Defries made a brief hop at Sydney on 9 December 1909 and Ralph Banks one on 1 March 1910, so 'first to fly in Australia' turns on what counts as a flight. The Museums Victoria collections article could not be re-fetched this pass because of a server block; the Aerial League record is corroborated elsewhere.
stops.campa: On a paddock northwest of Melbourne, after days of waiting out the wind, Houdini takes the Voisin up three times, circles, and puts it down where he started. The longest run is seven minutes thirty-seven seconds over about six miles. Witnesses sign certificates on the spot and the Aerial League of Australia gives him a trophy for the first extended controlled powered flight made in the country. Colin Defries had already lifted a Wright machine off a Sydney racecourse the previous December. It depends what a flight is.
suggested_refs: Aerial League of Australia trophy and witness certificates, Diggers Rest, March 1910
Museums Victoria collections, Houdini's Australian flights
sources: Museums Victoria collections article on Houdini's Australian flights

stops.name: The East River off lower Manhattan: nailed into the box
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia and the PBS timeline. Coordinate corrected: the pool's pin lay in Upper New York Bay off Battery Park, the wrong water. Wikipedia states plainly that he first performed the escape in New York's East River on 7 July 1912, so the pin is moved into the East River off lower Manhattan.
stops.campa: The police refuse him a pier, so he hires a tug and takes the whole thing out onto the river instead. He is handcuffed, put in leg irons, nailed into a wooden packing case weighted with iron, roped around, and swung over the side. He is on the surface in under a minute. The reporters go over the box more carefully than they go over the man, which is the correct instinct and gets them nowhere. The box has come back up still nailed, still roped, and still weighted with its iron.
suggested_refs: The overboard packing box, weighted and nailed, later a standing feature of the American tours

stops.name: Circus Busch, Berlin: the Water Torture Cell, first performed as a play
stops.date_confidence: Date and venue attested by Wikipedia and the PBS timeline. Coordinate flagged: Circus Busch's permanent building stood at Am Zirkus 1 off Schiffbauerdamm in Berlin-Mitte, approximately 52.5225, 13.3856; the pool's latitude placed the pin some 650 metres north of the Spree. No German address source was reachable this pass, so the corrected latitude should be verified before publication.
stops.campa: He calls the apparatus USD, for Upside Down. Ankles locked into a mahogany-framed stock, he is hoisted, inverted, and lowered head first into a glass-fronted tank of water; the stock is padlocked down onto the top and a curtain closes over it. The word Chinese in the name is marketing and has no China in it. He debuts the thing in Berlin as a one-act play called Houdini Upside Down, performed once before a paying audience, because British copyright law will protect a drama and will not protect a trick.
suggested_refs: The Chinese Water Torture Cell, its frame surviving the 1995 Niagara Falls, Ontario museum fire and restored by John Gaughan

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street: Cecelia Weiss dies while he is at sea
stops.date_confidence: Death date and place attested. Houdini was touring in Europe and was NOT at this pin on this date; the reachable record does not name the city where the news reached him, so rather than stage him somewhere unsupported the stop is placed at the house where she died and to which he returned. The gap is the point.
stops.campa: Cecelia Weiss dies in the Harlem house on the seventeenth of July. Her son is somewhere in Europe, working, and the record does not say in which city the cable finds him. He comes back across the Atlantic. After this the escapes go on exactly as before, the same cabinet, the same cuffs, the same money. Every seance he attends for the next thirteen years is a test of whether a message from this woman is possible, and the answer he keeps getting is no.
stops.quote: IF GOD IN HIS INFINITE WISDOM EVER SENT AN ANGEL UPON EARTH IN HUMAN FORM IT WAS MY MOTHER
stops.quote_source: Harry Houdini, dedication page of A Magician Among the Spirits (New York, 1924), set in full capitals
suggested_refs: The dedication page of A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), printed in capitals across the width of the page
sources: Harry Houdini, A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), Project Gutenberg #66451

stops.name: Flatbush, Brooklyn: the only recording of his voice
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Public Domain Review's presentation of the cylinders and by cylinder-restoration reporting. The Flatbush studio is named by the source; the street address is not.
stops.campa: In a Flatbush studio he records practice introductions for the Water Torture Cell onto wax cylinders, running the same patter over and over to get it right, and adds family material and some recitation. What the machine catches is not an escape. It is the sales pitch that frames one: the flat, fast, hurrying delivery of a man who has spent fifteen years throwing his voice to the back of a hall, describing an apparatus he will be lowered into head first that same week. These are the only recordings of him anyone has found.
suggested_refs: The 1914 Houdini wax cylinders, presented and restored by the Public Domain Review
Edison-type wax cylinder phonograph recording of the period
sources: Public Domain Review, 'Houdini on His Water Torture Cell'

stops.name: Near Santa Ana, California: six feet of earth and no coffin
stops.date_confidence: Year attested from Houdini's own diary as quoted in Silverman and Begley; month and day unknown, defaulted. The exact site outside Santa Ana is not recorded.
stops.campa: He has himself buried in six feet of earth with no coffin, meaning to dig his own way up through it. The soil is heavier than he calculated. He loses his sense of which way the surface is, panics, calls out and gets dirt in his mouth for it, and gets one hand through into the air before the men above can reach him. They pull him out barely conscious. His diary calls the weight killing and the feat very dangerous. He never does it again in open ground.
suggested_refs: Houdini's diary entry on the Santa Ana burial, quoted in Silverman and Begley
sources: Adam Begley, Houdini: The Elusive American (2020)

stops.name: The New York Hippodrome, Sixth Avenue: the elephant and the draft card
stops.date_confidence: Hippodrome engagement attested for 1917 to 1918; month and day defaulted. Election as national president of the Society of American Magicians is attested for 1917. The draft registration of 12 September 1918 as 'Harry Handcuff Houdini' is from the National Archives Atlanta WWI draft card collection; the card images are confirmed to exist but the full transcription was not independently verified this pass.
stops.campa: At the Hippodrome, a theater seating thousands, he makes a live elephant disappear twice a day. In the same stretch he is elected national president of the Society of American Magicians, an office he holds until he dies, and he registers for the wartime draft under the name Harry Handcuff Houdini, occupation actor and manager. He sells war bonds, later credited at more than a million dollars, and teaches soldiers how to get out of German handcuffs. His first film serial, The Master Mystery, is shot the same year.
suggested_refs: Houdini's WWI draft registration card, National Archives, Atlanta
The Master Mystery (1918), fifteen-part serial produced by B. A. Rolfe
sources: National Archives Atlanta, WWI draft card collection
Society of American Magicians institutional history

segments.name: Los Angeles and the Patent Office

stops.name: Laurel Canyon, Los Angeles: the estate that was never his
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a period, 1918 to 1920, during the Famous Players-Lasky films; a mid-period year is used and month and day defaulted. Houdini's actual rented address was not confirmed, so the pin is general Laurel Canyon. The correction that the so-called Houdini Estate at 2400 Laurel Canyon belonged to Ralph M. Walker is widely documented in Los Angeles historical and real-estate press.
stops.campa: Under contract to Famous Players-Lasky he rents quarters in Laurel Canyon and trains at a neighbouring property belonging to his friend and business associate Ralph Walker. The pictures do moderate business. He is not much of an actor and the camera flattens the thing he is best at, but he does his own stunts, hanging off a moving car and out of an aeroplane. The grand estate at 2400 Laurel Canyon, sold and resold for a century as the Houdini Estate, was Walker's house. Houdini never owned it.
suggested_refs: The Grim Game (1919), lost for 96 years, restored print premiered on Turner Classic Movies in 2015
Ralph M. Walker's Laurel Canyon property, marketed since as the Houdini Estate
sources: Los Angeles historical and real-estate press on the Walker property

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street: a diver's suit you can get out of
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the patent itself: application filed 30 June 1917, granted 1 March 1921 as US Patent 1,370,316. No workshop address appears on the patent, so the pin is the Harlem house where he kept his apparatus.
stops.campa: He patents a diver's suit built to be taken off under water. It comes in two parts with a quick-release joint at the waist, so that a diver in trouble can climb out of the bottom half and swim clear of it before he drowns. It is his own escape act pointed at somebody else's survival, drawn from fifteen years of getting out of things while holding his breath. He files it in June 1917, with the war on, and the patent issues in March 1921 as number 1,370,316. No navy takes it up.
suggested_refs: US Patent 1,370,316, diver's suit, filed 30 June 1917, granted 1 March 1921

stops.name: The Ambassador Hotel, Atlantic City: fifteen pages in English
stops.date_confidence: Date contradiction, unresolved and internal to the sources. Houdini's own witnessed statement and his printed account in A Magician Among the Spirits give 17 June 1922, his mother's birthday, and that is the date used here. wildabouthoudini.com argues from Houdini's own detailed notes that the seance was Sunday 18 June and that his public statement misdated it. Coordinate corrected: the Ambassador stood at 2831 Boardwalk, the site now occupied by the Tropicana, 39.3523, -74.4456; the pool's pin sat 1.6 km up the Boardwalk.
stops.campa: In a suite beside the Doyles', Lady Jean Conan Doyle takes up a pencil, prays, and begins to write. She fills about fifteen pages with a message from Cecelia Weiss, headed with a cross. Arthur Conan Doyle believes it entirely and believes his friend has just been handed the thing every bereaved man wants. Houdini sits there and is visibly moved, and takes up a pencil himself. Then he goes away and thinks about it for six months, and what he thinks about is the language it is written in.
stops.quote: Oh, my darling, thank God, thank God, at last I'm through--I've tried, oh, so often--now I am happy.
stops.quote_source: Lady Jean Conan Doyle, automatic writing at Atlantic City, printed verbatim by Houdini in A Magician Among the Spirits (New York, 1924), ch. IX
suggested_refs: The fifteen automatic-writing pages of 18 June 1922, reproduced in A Magician Among the Spirits, ch. IX
sources: Harry Houdini, A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), Project Gutenberg #66451, ch. IX

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street: the letter to Crowborough
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Houdini printed the letter himself, dated 15 December 1922 and addressed to Windlesham, Crowborough, Sussex. The pool cited a blog for two quotations Houdini published in his own book, and silently repunctuated both; the book text is restored here. The writing address is not stated in the letter, so the pin is his house.
stops.campa: Six months after Atlantic City he writes to Sussex to explain himself. His mother was born in Hungary, kept a rabbi's household, spoke German and Yiddish and Hungarian, and could not read, write, or speak English. The message runs fifteen fluent English pages. It is also headed with a cross, on the widow of a rabbi, on a day that happened to be her birthday and went unmentioned in it. He is careful and courteous and gives Doyle every allowance except the one that matters. The friendship does not survive the letter.
stops.quote: I know you are honorable and sincere and think I owe you an explanation regarding the letter I received through the hands of Lady Doyle.
stops.quote_source: Harry Houdini to Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, 15 December 1922, printed in A Magician Among the Spirits (New York, 1924), ch. IX
suggested_refs: The Houdini-Doyle correspondence, Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin
sources: Harry Houdini, A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), Project Gutenberg #66451, ch. IX

stops.name: St. Cecile Lodge No. 568, Manhattan: initiated
stops.date_confidence: Correction to the research pool: freemason.com gives only the year 1923 for the initiation, not the precise date of 17 July 1923 the pool carried, so the date is reduced to the year and defaulted. The raisings on 31 July and 21 August 1924 are confirmed. The Scottish Rite Cathedral used for the benefit is not separately addressed by the source, so both events share the Masonic Hall pin.
stops.campa: He is initiated into Freemasonry at St. Cecile Lodge No. 568, raised through the degrees over two days the following summer, and goes on into the Scottish Rite and the Mecca Shrine. He gives a benefit for the Scottish Rite Valley of New York in front of some four thousand brothers and raises relief money for Masons in trouble. In these same months he is the most aggressive public enemy the American spiritualist movement has. Whether anyone in the lodge ever put those two things to him as a question, the records do not say.
suggested_refs: St. Cecile Lodge No. 568 records, New York, 1923-1924

stops.name: 278 West 113th Street: the book against the mediums
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested and consistent across bibliographies; month and day unknown, defaulted. Text read directly from Project Gutenberg #66451.
stops.campa: He writes the book out of his own library: the Fox sisters, slate writing, spirit photography, medium after medium taken apart method by method, and the fourteen compacts he made with dying friends that whichever went first would send word back. The dedication runs across the page in capitals, to his mother. The book does not claim that the dead cannot speak. It claims that in thirty years of looking, with better equipment and less credulity than anyone else in the field, he has never once seen it happen.
stops.quote: I have made compacts with fourteen different persons that whichever of us died first would communicate with the other if it were possible, but I have never received a word.
stops.quote_source: Harry Houdini, A Magician Among the Spirits (New York, 1924)
suggested_refs: Harry Houdini, Miracle Mongers and Their Methods (1920), the earlier volume on fire-eaters and stage marvels
sources: Harry Houdini, A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), Project Gutenberg #66451

stops.name: Boston: the sittings with Margery
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the PBS timeline; month inferred to place the sittings before the pamphlet of November 1924. The Crandon house on Lime Street is where the sittings were held but is not given a coordinate by the reachable sources, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: The Scientific American offers a prize for demonstrable psychic phenomena and the committee's strongest candidate is Mina Crandon, a Boston surgeon's wife who sits as Margery and produces the voice of her dead brother Walter. Houdini joins the sittings and builds a wooden control cabinet that leaves her head and hands outside it and the rest of her where he can account for it. The phenomena stop. He reports that she rings the bell box with her foot. The committee votes against her, and Boston, which is fond of her, does not forgive him. In November he prints a pamphlet at his own expense and gives it away.
suggested_refs: The Margery control cabinet, built by Houdini for the Scientific American committee, 1924
Houdini Exposes the Tricks Used by the Boston Medium 'Margery' (privately printed, November 1924)

stops.name: Symphony Hall, Boston: the exposure staged as a show
stops.date_confidence: Attested to January 1925 by PBS, 'The Margery Pamphlet', with the Crandon reply at Jordan Hall days later and the committee's decision in February; day of month not recorded, defaulted.
stops.campa: He hires Symphony Hall, puts the cabinet on the stage, and shows a paying audience exactly how the Margery effects are produced. The pamphlet has already been printed at his own expense and given away. The Crandon side answers at Jordan Hall a few days later, in front of their own crowd, and both sides sell tickets to the argument. The question of whether the dead can speak is now a question of which of two living parties is lying. In February the committee formally denies her the prize.
suggested_refs: Jordan Hall, Boston, where the Crandon side answered days later

stops.name: Washington, before the subcommittee
stops.date_confidence: Hearings ran February to May 1926; the stop is dated to the opening month. Correction to the research pool: its geography lens named only a House subcommittee, while the PBS timeline says he testified before Senate and House subcommittees, so both chambers are carried. The hearing room is not identified, and the pin marks the House office building generally.
stops.campa: He comes to testify for H.R. 8989, a bill to make it a crime to take money for telling fortunes in the District of Columbia, and tells the subcommittee flatly that every medium he has ever tested was a fraud. The room fills with mediums and their defenders and they shout him down. Jane Coates and a fortune teller called Madam Marcia give evidence against him. He has brought his own exhibits and does tricks at the witness table to make his point. The bill fails.
suggested_refs: Jeremy C. Young, 'Empowering Passivity: Women Spiritualists, Houdini, and the 1926 Fortune Telling Hearing', Journal of Social History 48.2 (2014)
Houdini's preserved hearing testimony, Harry Ransom Center finding aid
sources: Jeremy C. Young, Journal of Social History 48.2 (2014)

stops.name: The Hotel Shelton pool, Lexington Avenue: ninety-one minutes in a casket
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The Shelton Hotel stood at 525 Lexington Avenue at the southeast corner of East 49th Street; the coordinate is corrected from the pool's, which was about 390 metres off. Wikipedia's Shelton Hotel article gives the duration as 91 minutes, so 91 is used rather than the pool's 'about ninety'.
stops.campa: An Egyptian performer calling himself Rahman Bey has lain sealed in a coffin under water for an hour and credited a trance state for it. Houdini is fifty-two, out of condition, and no kind of swimmer. He has a galvanized casket built, gets into it, and is lowered into the hotel swimming pool with the lid soldered down. He stays under ninety-one minutes, breathing shallow and lying still, and comes up soaked in sweat and able to speak. His explanation is that anyone calm enough could do it.
suggested_refs: Rahman Bey's sealed-coffin demonstrations of 1926, the provocation for the Shelton test
sources: Adam Begley, Houdini: The Elusive American (2020)

stops.name: Worcester YMCA: seventy-one minutes, for the third act
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The repeat test at the Worcester YMCA on 28 September 1926 and the duration of about seventy-one minutes come from Silverman and Begley and were not independently re-verified against a Worcester source this pass.
stops.campa: He repeats the sealed-casket test in the pool of the Worcester YMCA and stays under about seventy-one minutes, timed. It is not a booking, there is no house to split with, and nobody sells a ticket. He is assembling a full evening show against spiritualism for the coming season, three acts, magic and then escapes and then the exposure, and this is research for the third act. The ankle he will be lying on a couch with in Montreal, four weeks from now, is not yet broken.
suggested_refs: Houdini's three-act anti-spiritualism programme, in preparation for the 1926-1927 season
sources: Adam Begley, Houdini: The Elusive American (2020)

stops.name: The Princess Theatre, Montreal: four or five blows in the dressing room
stops.date_confidence: Date, place, the assailant, and the witness account attested by history.com, 'What Killed Harry Houdini?'. Coordinate flagged: the Princess Theatre stood at 480 Ste-Catherine Street West, approximately 45.5045, -73.5680, and the pool's pin was some 500 metres north; no Wikipedia article for the theatre exists to check the address against, so it should be verified before publication.
stops.campa: He is lying on a couch in the dressing room with a fractured ankle propped up, going through his mail, when three McGill students come in. One of them, J. Gordon Whitehead, asks whether it is true that he can take any blow to the stomach. Before Houdini has properly stood or set himself, Whitehead hits him four or five times, hard, deliberately, well directed. Jacques Price and Sam Smilovitz, the other two, put down in writing afterward what they saw. Houdini finishes the engagement and gets on the train.
stops.quote: four or five terribly forcible, deliberate, well-directed blows
stops.quote_source: Sam Smilovitz, witness statement on the Montreal dressing-room assault, quoted in history.com, 'What Killed Harry Houdini?'
suggested_refs: The Price and Smilovitz witness statements, Montreal, October 1926

stops.name: The Garrick Theatre, Detroit: the last performance
stops.date_confidence: Attested by history.com, including the fever near 104 degrees Fahrenheit and the medical advice to go to hospital, which he refused until after the show.
stops.campa: He arrives in Detroit with a temperature near a hundred and four and a doctor telling him to go straight to a hospital. He goes to the theater. He gets through the first act, has the curtain brought down while an assistant packs him in ice, and goes back out and finishes. The house is told nothing. It is the last performance of a working life that has run thirty-two years without a season off, and he plays it with a burst appendix. Afterward he lets them take him to Grace Hospital.
suggested_refs: The Garrick Theatre, Detroit, and the programme for the week of 24 October 1926

stops.name: Grace Hospital, Detroit: Halloween
stops.date_confidence: Cause and date of death attested by Wikipedia and the Jewish Virtual Library. The hour of about 1:26 p.m. and the bedside detail come from history.com and the Archives of Michigan death-certificate record cited in the pool, which was not independently read this pass, so they are reconstruction. The causal relation between the Montreal blows and the appendicitis is medically disputed and is left disputed.
stops.campa: They open him and find the appendix ruptured and gangrenous and the abdomen full of pus. There are no antibiotics in 1926. Peritonitis on this scale is not survivable and the surgeons know it while they are still operating. He lives six days. Whether Whitehead's blows tore an appendix that was already infected, or whether the appendicitis was independent and the assault only fixed a date in everyone's mind, has never been settled. He dies on Halloween at about half past one, with Bess and his brothers in the room.
suggested_refs: Archives of Michigan death-certificate record for Harry Houdini, 31 October 1926
The medical literature disputing the causal role of the Montreal blows

stops.name: Machpelah Cemetery, Queens: the family plot and the broken wand
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate corrected and an internal contradiction in the research pool resolved: its geography lens gave 40.6994, -73.8968 and its afterlife lens 40.6975, -73.8809 for the same cemetery; Wikipedia gives 40.69389, -73.88639, which is used.
stops.campa: More than two thousand people come. He is buried in the Weiss family plot beside his mother and his father, the rabbi who never held a second pulpit, under a monument carrying the crest of the Society of American Magicians. Magicians break a wand over the grave. Bess, raised Catholic, wanted to lie beside him and does not; when she dies in 1943 she is buried thirty-five miles north in Westchester. The bust set over him in 1927 will be smashed or stolen four times in eighteen years.
suggested_refs: The Society of American Magicians broken-wand service, held at the grave annually
The 1927 bust, damaged or stolen on four occasions between 1975 and 1993, and the replacement installed unannounced by the Houdini Museum of Scranton on 27 September 2011
Gate of Heaven Cemetery, Hawthorne, New York, where Bess Houdini was buried in 1943
